scenes.title: Prologue — The Hive, remembered
scenes.prose: Night. Rain. An eleven-storey block of balconies and wires wedged between glass towers.

dialogueBeats.text: This is how I remember it.
After the war they raised a block beside the railway, to house the factories. The factories closed. We stayed.
We built upward. A room for a daughter. A shop for a brother. A stair, a pipe, a balcony bolted onto a balcony. Sixty years, until nobody could say where the factory ended and we began.
The city grew up around us, and forgot we were here. That was all right. We were busy.
Now the land is worth more than we are. Everything is going. We are just slower.

scenes.title: 1 — The backstreet

dialogueBeats.text: Rain. Not a storm. Just cold, steady, patient rain.
A narrow street of shuttered shops.
A vending machine hums on the corner. High up, one lit window, a radio playing behind it.
MARA VOSS (24) walks fast, arms folded, soaked, no umbrella.
Her phone lights up: VERA. She watches it ring.
Not tonight.
She declines it.

THE SCRAP

The note in her hands. Her handwriting, in biro: 1.00 Sakai. Underneath is an address. Beneath that, underlined twice: "just listen."
She looks down the lane. At the far end, the bar sign. She checks her watch (12.45). Early.
The rain thickens.
She slips into the barbershop doorway, behind the scooter and the crates, and presses back into the shadow to shelter from the rain.
The beer crates will hide her from anyone in the lane. She hopes. She isn't sure she wants to walk in at all.
Somewhere nearby, a pedestrian crossing CHIMES its old melody for an empty intersection. Over and over. No one crosses.
Footsteps. Hurried. Uneven.
An OLD MAN (70s) in a cheap raincoat and a grey flat cap comes in from the road, one hand pressed to his side as if something is hidden there.
He keeps looking back.
Mara sees him. Looks at the scrap.
She leans out of the shadow. The red bird clip catches the street light.
He sees it. He stops, six metres short of her. For one second his whole face changes.
Then he shakes his head. Barely. A man refusing a stranger. And he turns his back on her, slowly, to face the road.
Behind him, at the mouth of the lane, headlights. A black sedan pulls across the opening and stops, blocking it.
Its high beams shine straight down the lane, lighting the rain in long white columns.
Two MEN get out and walk in, black silhouettes against the glare. Black clothes. Masks. They don't run.
The old man doesn't move.
He stands between them and Mara's doorway, a small figure in the white light, his shadow stretching long down the lane toward her.
After twenty years.
A suppressed SHOT.
Flat and ordinary, like a door closing.
The old man folds onto the street.
One of the masked men touches his ear.
First position done. Moving to second.
They walk back to the sedan. They don't hurry. They never look at the doorway.
It pulls away and takes the long way round the block, its high beams swinging off the lane.
Mara runs to the old man. Her bag slides off her shoulder and spills across the wet street. She doesn't notice.
Mr. Sakai?
Hold on, I'll call an ambulance.
His hand comes out of his coat with something small and brass in it. He presses it into her palm and closes her fingers over it.
Don't let them have it.
Have what? I don't —
He's gone. Rain in his open eyes.
In her hand: a small brass key on a stamped number tag.
At the other end of the street, the amber glow of a bar. Mara runs for it.
Behind her, on the street: her purse, open in the rain.

scenes.title: 2 — The small bar

dialogueBeats.text: Six stools and a counter. Shelves of bottles glowing amber.
On a high shelf, an old CRT television plays a late-night variety show, sound low. Rain drums on the roof.
A man in a raincoat on the far stool, a notebook beside a beer gone flat: the JOURNALIST (40s). Nobody behind the counter.
Crates clatter somewhere in the back.
Mara bursts in, the key in her fist.
Miss Voss?
He knows her name.
Are you okay? Where's Sakai?
Before she can answer, the door opens behind her. Rain noise.
Shitsurei shimasu. (Excuse me.)
Mara is behind the counter before she knows she's moved.
Two men in masks, inside the door. The journalist doesn't get up.
Two shots.
On the high shelf, the television audience laughs.
Behind the counter, Mara folds herself into the gap between the crates and the ice bin.
A hair clip slides out of her wet hair and skitters under the shelf. She doesn't breathe.
Second position done.
He takes one step toward the counter. A voice in his earpiece: one word. He turns and goes.
The door swings shut. The television laughs again.
MAIN TITLES

scenes.title: 3 — Three days later

dialogueBeats.text: THREE DAYS LATER
An old four-story apartment block squeezed between newer buildings.
Laundry left out on a balcony, getting rained on.
A train slides past on the elevated line behind it, windows lit, and the whole building trembles faintly.
One window on the third floor is lit.

scenes.title: 4 — Vera's apartment

dialogueBeats.text: Small and tidy. Grey light through rain-streaked glass. A smartphone on the table; an old boxy television in the corner.
Nothing here quite belongs to one decade.
By the door, in the umbrella stand: a pale blue umbrella. Bone dry.
On a shelf, one framed photograph, its colors gone warm and faded. A Tokyo street, twenty years ago.
An American man in a rumpled suit, smiling, holding the hands of two small girls: VERA (9), serious, and MARA (4), mid-laugh.
Behind them, the sign of a noodle shop.
VERA VOSS (29) sits at the low table.
Two cups. Hers holds cold tea.
The other is empty and clean, set out as though someone is expected.
Through the thin wall, a neighbour's radio plays an old ballad, muffled: a woman's voice, a song from another decade.
Vera doesn't seem to hear it.
Her phone lies face up in front of her. She calls. Waits.
It's Mara. You know what to do.
BEEP.
Vera opens her mouth. For a moment, nothing.
It's me again. I'm not angry anymore. I wasn't really angry then, either. Whatever that man wants, it doesn't matter.
I just — You left your umbrella. You'll get soaked.
Just call me. You don't have to say anything. Just call, so I know.
She hangs up.
The old television murmurs to itself.

...police in Kanda are investigating a double shooting in a small bar in the early hours of Sunday. Two men were killed. Officers say it appears to be a dispute between criminal groups. No arrests have been made...
...rain continuing through the rest of the week...
She looks at the umbrella by the door. At the clean, empty cup. At the photograph.
She stands. Puts on her coat. Hesitates at the door.
Then she takes the blue umbrella. Mara's umbrella.
The door closes behind her. Through the wall, the song on the neighbour's radio ends. A DJ murmurs something. Rain.

scenes.title: 5 — The front counter
scenes.prose: INT. POLICE STATION, FRONT COUNTER - NIGHT

dialogueBeats.text: Fluorescent tubes, one of them flickering. A long counter. Faded posters about pickpockets and traffic safety.
An old fax machine beside a new flat monitor. A wall clock that runs a minute fast.
Vera stands at the counter, the closed blue umbrella dripping onto the linoleum.
A YOUNG OFFICER takes her details with polite boredom.
Vera's Japanese is fluent, but careful and slightly formal — learned as a child, relearned as an adult.
Your sister's age?
Twenty-four.
Adults sometimes go away for a few days. Especially foreigners. It's usually —
She doesn't. Not without telling me.
He types the name. ON THE MONITOR: MARA VOSS.
He stops typing.
He looks at the screen a moment too long. Then he picks up the desk phone and turns away from her.
Yes. That name. Yes — the sister is here now.
He hangs up. His manner has changed. Politer.
Someone will be right with you.
Vera looks at him. He doesn't meet her eyes.

scenes.title: 6 — The interview room
scenes.prose: INT. POLICE STATION, INTERVIEW ROOM - MOMENTS LATER

dialogueBeats.text: Small. A table, two chairs, a box of tissues nobody has touched in years. Rain on a frosted window.
DETECTIVE ISHIDA (50s) sets a paper cup of tea in front of Vera. Gentle. Unhurried. Tired, in a way that looks like decency.
You must be cold.
His English is excellent.
I speak Japanese.
Of course. But this is a difficult thing. It is easier in your own language.
A small beat. She lets it go. For now.
The officer made a phone call the moment he had my sister's name. Then you came.
A foreign passport. We like to take care with these things.
He slides a form across the table, and a pen. MISSING PERSON, in Japanese, with an English line beneath.
Name. Height. What she was wearing, if you know.
She fills it in. Her handwriting is fast and square. Ishida reads it upside down as she writes, without seeming to.
Voss. You grew up here?
Until I was nine.
And your parents? They are in America?
My mother is. My father died.
Here?
Here. When I was a child.
I'm sorry. Did your sister ever talk about him?
The pen stops.
She was four. She doesn't remember him.
It is not quite an answer. Ishida lets it be one.
A recent photograph?
Vera takes her wallet from her bag.
From behind her card, a small square passport photo: MARA, unsmiling for once, a strand of hair across her eyes.
She gave me two when she renewed. In case.
In case.
He takes it by the edges. Looks at it a moment. Sets it on the form, squares it to the corner.
When did you last see her?
Thursday. At my apartment. We had dinner.
And how did she seem?
Vera hesitates.
Normal.
Ishida waits, kindly, as if he knows there is more. She doesn't give it.
Did she ever speak of your family? Anything she had been thinking about?
No.
Did she mention Kanda? Friends there? Work?
Kanda? No. Why —
She stops. Something arrives in her face.
The shootings. In Kanda. It was on the news.
Ishida says nothing. That is its own answer.
Is she hurt?
We have no reason to believe she is hurt.
That's not the same as saying she isn't.
Miss Voss —
Is she dead?
We have no reason to believe so.
She hears it: the careful, official shape of the sentence. Her hand tightens around the paper cup.
Stop saying that. Stop saying what you have no reason to believe and tell me what you know.
The cup crumples in her fist. Hot tea runs over her fingers and onto the table, across the corner of the form. She doesn't seem to feel it.

What I know is that two men were killed in Kanda, and that it is a matter between criminal groups. And that your sister is a young woman who has not called her sister for three days. Those may be two separate things.
May be.
May be.
Ishida takes a tissue from the box, the first in years, and offers it. She doesn't take it. He sets it down beside her hand.
When she speaks again, it's in Japanese. Low. Precise. Every word placed.
She is my sister. I have been calling her for days. If you know where she is, tell me.
Ishida looks at her a long moment. When he answers, it is in Japanese too, for the first time. Formal. A door closing.

I do not know where she is. That is the truth. And if, on the off chance, she did see something she should not have, then the safest place for her is wherever she is now. And the safest thing you can do is nothing.
Silence. Rain on the frosted window.
He switches back to English, gentle again, as if the last minute didn't happen.
Go home, Miss Voss. Keep your phone on. If she calls, call me first. Any hour.
He slides his card across the wet table. She looks at it. Then takes it. Stands. Picks up the blue umbrella.
At the door:
You would have told me if she was dead. Wouldn't you?
Of course, I'm sure we will find her, you have my word.
She looks at him. She can't tell. She goes. The door closes behind her.
Ishida sits alone a moment. He wipes the spilled tea from the table with the tissue, slowly, carefully, until there is no trace of it.
Then he picks up the passport photo, dry at the edges, looks at Mara's face, and slides it into his inside pocket.
The form he leaves where it is.

scenes.title: 7 — The detectives' room
scenes.prose: INT. POLICE STATION, DETECTIVES' ROOM - CONTINUOUS

dialogueBeats.text: Rows of cluttered desks under humming fluorescent light. Most are empty at this hour. A radio plays low somewhere.
Ishida sits at his desk and opens the bottom drawer. The two drawers above it stay closed.

THE DRAWER

Inside the drawer, sealed together in one clear evidence bag: Mara's purse and the torn strap, coiled beside it. Still damp.
He looks at it a long moment.
Closes the drawer.
On the wall, the clock runs a minute fast.

scenes.title: 8 — We're closed

dialogueBeats.text: The same bar in flat grey daylight. It looks smaller without the night. Chairs up on the counter. The CRT television is dark.
Where the journalist fell, there is a new rubber floor mat, too clean for this room.
OKADA (60s), the bar's owner, mops around it without looking at it. He has the stillness of a man who hasn't slept.
The door opens. Vera, the blue umbrella in her hand.
We're closed.
Vera holds up her phone: a photo of Mara, laughing at a party, a paper crown on her head.
My sister. Four nights ago. Was she here?
Okada looks at the photo for exactly one second.
No.
You didn't look.
I looked. No.
His eyes go, just once, to the far end of the counter. Then back to the mop.
Vera sees it. She doesn't push. She bows, small and polite, and leaves.
She has left the blue umbrella leaning against a stool.
Okada looks at the umbrella for a long moment.

scenes.title: 9 — Behind the counter

dialogueBeats.text: Rain. Vera walks away down the narrow street, no umbrella, head down.
Miss.
She turns. Okada stands in the bar doorway holding the blue umbrella, out of breath, as if deciding something cost him more than the walk.
He hands it to her. Then he holds out his other hand. In it: the small red enamel bird clip.
Vera stops breathing.
It was mine. She took it when we were kids. She never gave it back.
She has said it in English, without realizing. Okada doesn't understand the words. He understands her face.
Behind the counter. After.
Did you give this to the police?
They didn't ask.
He takes a business card from his apron and presses it into her hand. Old, soft at the corners, handwritten on the back.
Not the police. Him.
Who is he?
He found my daughter once. When no one else would look.
He goes back inside before she can thank him.
Vera looks at the card. Printed in English and in katakana: JACK. INVESTIGATIONS. An address. No surname.

scenes.title: 10 — Depends who's calling

dialogueBeats.text: Second floor of an old building pressed against the elevated railway. One room.
Frosted glass door, JACK hand-lettered on it in English and in katakana.
A desk. A black rotary phone. Filing cabinets. A small CRT television on the cabinet, muted, playing an old black-and-white samurai film.
A sofa that has clearly been slept on.
A TRAIN passes outside. The blinds shiver. A spoon rattles in an empty cup. Then silence again.
JACK (48) sits at the desk eating a convenience-store rice ball, watching the silent swordsmen.
Handsome once, in a way he stopped maintaining. A good coat, badly kept. He flicks an old steel lighter open and shut, open and shut.
There are no cigarettes anywhere.
A knock on the frosted glass. Vera comes in, wet, the blue umbrella dripping.
Are you the one they call Jack?
Depends who's calling.
Mr. Okada. The bar in Kanda.
Jack puts the rice ball down.
Sit down.
She sits. He doesn't switch to English. He lets her speak in the language she chose. She notices.
My sister has been missing for four days. The police say to go home and wait.
I don't do missing persons. People who go missing usually want to.
She places the red bird clip on his desk.
She was in that bar. The night two men were shot there.
Jack looks at the clip for a long moment. The lighter stops.
What did the police tell you?
To go home.
It's good advice.
Is it yours, too?
He doesn't answer. Another train passes. The blinds shiver.
Do you have photographs of her?
She takes an envelope from her bag. As she pulls out the photos, something slides out with them and falls face up on the desk:
The old framed photograph from her shelf, taken out of its frame. Twenty years ago. The American man in the rumpled suit.
The two small girls. The noodle shop sign behind them.
Jack looks at it.
He does not move. On the TV behind him, a sword is drawn in total silence.
That's us. Before we left.
She has slipped into English. So does he, quietly.
Your father.
He died. That year. Here.
Jack picks the photograph up by its edges, carefully, the way you'd handle evidence. Or something fragile.
He looks a moment too long at the noodle shop sign. Then he sets it down, face up, and squares it to the edge of the desk.
I'm sorry.
It was a long time ago.
Yes.
A beat.
Ten thousand yen a day. Plus expenses. I'll need a key to her apartment, her phone number, her friends, where she worked, where she drank.
So you'll look.
I'll look.
She gathers the photographs, and the red bird clip with them. He watches it go back into her pocket. He doesn't ask for it.
At the door, she stops.
Mr. Okada said you found his daughter.
I found her.
Was she alive?
Jack looks at her. The honest answer is in the pause.
Her Japanese. Your sister's. Is it good?
Some. Badly.
Then she stands out. That helps.
Vera nods. Goes. Through the frosted glass, her shape goes down the stairs and is gone.
Jack sits very still.

scenes.title: 11 — Two men laughing

dialogueBeats.text: Past midnight. Only the desk lamp and the grey flicker of the television, now showing static.
Jack crouches at the grey steel cupboard under the window, pulls its door open and takes out a cardboard box he has kept behind the files.
Dust on the lid. He hasn't opened it in years.
Inside: a police notebook. An old ID card with a younger face. A folded newspaper clipping.

THE CLIPPING

An English-language newspaper, yellowed. A small headline: AMERICAN INSURANCE INVESTIGATOR FOUND DEAD - POLICE RULE SUICIDE.
A photograph: the same man from Vera's picture. The caption: DANIEL VOSS, 41.
Beneath the clipping, one more photograph.
Two men at a tiny noodle counter, laughing, steam in the air: DANIEL VOSS, and a much younger JACK, still in a cheap police-issue suit.
Behind them, the same noodle shop sign.
Jack looks at it for a long time.
Then he dials the rotary phone. It takes a long time to dial.
It's late, Jack.
The Voss girl came to see me.
I know.
Silence on the line. Rain on the window.
Her sister was in that bar.
The sister is a missing persons case. The bar is a gang matter. Two separate things.
And the old man in the street?
Sakai. Yes. That Sakai. I know what you're thinking. Old debts, old enemies. It's a gang matter.
Twenty years, Ishida.
A long pause.
Go to sleep, Jack. You found enough twenty years ago. You're too old to be haunted.
The line goes dead.
Jack holds the receiver a moment longer. He sets it down.
Flicks the lighter open. Shut.
A train passes. The photograph of the two laughing men trembles on the desk.

scenes.title: 12 — The strap

dialogueBeats.text: The street from the cold open. The rain hasn't stopped in four days.
Jack walks it slowly, a cheap clear plastic umbrella over his head. Not searching. Looking.
The vending machine at the corner. He feeds it a coin. A can of hot coffee drops.
Thank you very much.
He holds the can without drinking it and looks at the spot where Sakai died. Nothing there now. Rain on asphalt.
He turns and looks at the barbershop doorway. Steps into it. Stands exactly where Mara stood.
From here, he can see the whole street. And, at the far end, the small lit sign of Okada's bar.
He looks at the barbershop pole beside him. Crouches.
Caught on a rough metal edge at knee height: a short twist of torn leather strap.
He doesn't touch it. He looks from the strap, to the spot where Sakai fell, to the bar sign. Reconstructing it.
A shutter RATTLES up above him. A BARBER (80s), in pajamas, looks down from the upstairs window.
Police again?
Not for a long time.
The barber considers him.
I told them. I was asleep. I heard the shot. Then a car.
One car?
One car. Twice. It left. Then it came back.
Jack looks down the empty street.
Why come back?
Nobody answers. He looks down the street at the drains, the doorways, the gutter: everywhere a small thing could fall.
The barber shrugs and pulls the shutter down.
He looks again at the doorway. At the bar sign. At the torn strap.
She was here. She saw it. She ran there. She saw that too.
And whatever they came back for, she has it.
He looks down the empty street at the bar sign.
And one more question he can't answer yet: what was an American girl doing in a Kanda backstreet at one in the morning?
Jack drops the unopened coffee into the recycling bin. The can CLANKS. The crossing melody starts up somewhere, for no one.

scenes.title: 14 — Someone who meant to come back

dialogueBeats.text: A tiny studio in an old building. Grey daylight. Clothes on every surface. Sketches taped to the walls: pencil, charcoal, cheap watercolour.
Trains. Rooftops. Laundry lines. Faces on the subway.
The room smells of someone who meant to come back.
Vera stands just inside the door. She hasn't taken her coat off. Jack moves through the room slowly, touching nothing yet. Looking.
When were you last here?
A week ago. She made me coffee. It was terrible.
Jack opens the fridge. Milk. A half-eaten cake in a box. He closes it.
She wasn't planning to disappear.
No.
He crouches by the futon. A suitcase underneath, packed and zipped. He looks at it, then at Vera.
That was for America. She'd booked a flight. Next month.
You didn't want her to go.
I didn't want her to run away again. That's what I said. The night she left. That she always runs.
She looks at the wall of drawings, not at him.
It was about Dad. It's always about Dad. She wanted to dig it all up. Who he was here. Why he — I told her to leave him dead. She said I was the one who ran.
All the way back here, chasing a ghost, and I won't even look at it.
I told her to go, then. Go home. Those were the last things I said to her.
Jack says nothing. He knows better than to comfort it away.
On the desk: a thick sketchbook, its cover soft with use. Jack opens it.
Page after page of the same place. A tiny noodle counter under a railway. Six stools. A curtain. A hand-painted sign.
Drawn over and over, from different angles, in different years of her hand — a child's crayon version taped inside the cover, the newest in careful ink.
She drew this a lot.
Vera glances over.
Since she was little. It's from a story I used to tell her. About the noodle shop Dad took us to. She was too young to remember it, so I told her. She made it up from what I said. It's not real.
Jack turns a page. The sign, in careful ink. Every stroke of the kanji correct.
He has seen this sign. Twice this week. Once in the photograph from Vera's shelf, on his own desk. Once in a box in his own cupboard.
Can I borrow this?
Why?
Jack doesn't answer. He looks at the drawing a moment too long.
Vera takes the hair clip out of her coat pocket and sets it on the sketchbook.
Take this too. It's mine. She stole it.
He takes both.
She hesitates, then nods. He closes the sketchbook and puts it under his arm, and says nothing else about it.

scenes.title: 14 — Forty metres

dialogueBeats.text: Rain. Wipers. Kanda's wet streets slide past the windscreen.
From the rear-view mirror, on a loop of string, the red bird clip swings with each turn.
In the mirror, behind it: a pair of headlights. The same distance, every turn. Never closer, never farther.
Jack watches them. One hand goes into his coat pocket and closes around the lighter. He takes a corner a shade too fast, then slow.
The headlights follow, dipped, patient.
He stops at the mouth of the lane, exactly where the sedan stopped, and kills the engine and lights.
Forty metres back, the headlights slow. Stop. Go out.
He waits, long enough to be sure. Then he gets out and walks back along the wet road toward the dark car, one hand in his pocket.
A small, boxy, maroon hatchback, its glass steamed. He raps on the driver's window with a knuckle.
It winds down. Vera, both hands on the wheel.
He takes his hand from his pocket. The old steel lighter, open, unlit.
Is that what you were holding?
It's what I had.
He snaps it shut.
Forty metres. Twenty minutes. You never once lost me.
Is that bad?
It's what a professional does.
Who did you think I was?
Somebody who'd be worse company.
You said you'd look. You didn't say where. I waited outside your office.
If you can follow me, so can they.
She hadn't thought of that. She looks past him at the empty road.
I brought food.
He sighs the sigh of a man who has lost an argument he was never allowed to make.
Park round the corner, then get in mine. One car is a man waiting. Two is somebody watching.
LATER. Engine off. Rain on the windscreen, no wipers; the glass turns the lane into smears of light.
At the far end, small and amber, the bar sign.
Vera shakes the blue umbrella out onto his floor. From a paper bag, two convenience-store rice balls. She holds one out.
You were eating one when I came in. I assumed it was a lifestyle.
This is a stakeout. Nothing happens.
Then I won't miss anything.
He takes it. Their fingers don't touch. Both notice that they don't.
They watch the lane.
What are we waiting for?
Whoever comes back.
Back?
Someone came back to this street that night. Nobody comes back for what they already have.
What didn't they have?
I don't know yet.
A TRAIN passes somewhere behind them. The mirror trembles, and the red bird swings. Vera watches it.
Is that for luck?
It's so I don't lose it.
A long silence. The rice ball in her lap, unwrapped, uneaten.
I told her she always runs.
You said.
It's the last thing I —
Runners don't pack. They leave with what they're wearing. Your sister had a suitcase zipped under the bed and a flight booked home. Whatever happened to her, she wasn't running from you.
You don't know that.
No. But I'd bet on it.
She looks at him for the first time since she sat down. He is looking at the lane. He doesn't look back.
A figure at the road end, under a black umbrella tilted low, face lost beneath it.
He walks past the car (both of them sink an inch in their seats) and into the lane.
He goes to the bar's shuttered door. Tries the handle. Stands under the amber sign, looking up and down the lane.
Then he turns back toward the road, and the umbrella swings toward the car.
Jack's arm goes out across Vera, pressing her back into the seat. Not looking. Reflex.
The umbrella holds on them. Then turns away. The man walks to a small white car further up the road, and gets in. He doesn't start it.
He sits.
Jack looks at his own arm, still across her chest, as if it belonged to someone else. He takes it back.
They sit very still. After a long time, the white car pulls out and goes, without hurry.
Jack finds a pencil stub, smooths the paper bag flat on his knee, and writes the plate number on it.
Is that routine? Watching a bar after a shooting?
Probably.
He folds the bag once and puts it inside his coat.
You don't think so.
We have a plate number.
3:40 a.m. The amber sign at the far end goes dark. Jack starts the engine.
Call me if you plan on going somewhere next time.
I will.
That's a lie.
Yes.
She sets the rice ball on his dashboard, still untouched, and gets out.
In the mirror he watches the blue umbrella go up the wet road and round the corner, and the dark take it.
A small engine starts, out of sight. Headlights swing across the end of the road and away. Jack counts ten.
Then he pulls out after them, forty metres back. Never closer. Never farther.

scenes.title: 15 — Forgotten by the city

dialogueBeats.text: Rain. A wide street of new glass towers and chain stores.
Between two towers, a long white construction hoarding: KUROSE DEVELOPMENT, and a painted plaza full of smiling people who don't exist.
Behind it, low and dark and patched, the Hive.

A dense, self-built block of stacked homes and workshops rising eleven storeys, balconies bolted onto balconies, air conditioners and pipes and laundry and hand-painted signs, all of it crushed together under the curve of the elevated railway.
The city has grown up around it and forgotten it is there.
At the back, the tower steps down to a low rear wing pressed hard against the concrete railway viaduct, its roof level with the tracks.
Old neon signs hang dead on its face.
Even in daylight the Hive sits in its own haze of steam and kitchen smoke, as if it had its own weather.
Jack stands on the pavement with the sketchbook under his coat. He looks up at the Hive for a long moment, as if at someone he used to know.
Then he goes in.

scenes.title: 16 — Everybody sees him

dialogueBeats.text: Narrow corridors, barely shoulder-wide, lit by bare bulbs. Water drips from somewhere above and runs along the floor in a thin shining line.
Pipes overhead. Wires everywhere. What daylight gets in comes in thin cold shafts from gaps far overhead, thick with drifting steam.
Doors stand open onto other lives. A MAN at a bench mending radios, a dozen of them murmuring different stations at once.
A FAMILY eating dinner at four in the afternoon, the TV loud. An OLD WOMAN asleep in front of a sumo match.
A dentist's chair behind a curtain, a hand-lettered price list taped to the wall.
Jack walks through it all. Nobody stops him. Everybody sees him.
A TRAIN passes overhead. The whole building trembles. Dust sifts down through the bulb light. Nobody looks up.
He turns a corner and stops.
The noodle counter. Six stools. The curtain. The hand-painted sign, faded almost to nothing but unmistakable.
It is exactly the drawing.

scenes.title: 17 — You got old

dialogueBeats.text: Steam. A single fluorescent tube. Two customers slurping in silence at the far end.
Behind the counter, KANEKO (70s), tiny and sharp-eyed, works a pot with long chopsticks. She looks up as Jack sits at the counter.
She looks at him for a long time. Longer than a stranger would.
You got old.
So did you.
I was already old. You were a boy in a cheap suit, the only foreign face on the force. Japanese papers, American face. You came here with the American.
Everything is going. We are just slower.
Jack looks at the counter under his hands.
I'm looking for his daughter. The younger one.
Kaneko's chopsticks don't pause.
The little one? She was four years old. She ate rice with her fingers.
She's twenty-four now. And someone wants to kill her.
The two customers at the end of the counter have stopped slurping.
Kaneko sets a bowl of noodles in front of Jack.
Eat. Then go. There is no one here but us.
Jack eats. Slowly. He finishes everything.
He puts down a little more than the bowl costs, and a business card on top of it.
He always paid too much, too.
He goes. Kaneko looks at the card for a long moment.
Behind the curtain, in the dark of the storeroom, something moves.

scenes.title: 18 — After the last train

dialogueBeats.text: Rain. The old television plays static. Jack sits in the dark, the sketchbook open on the desk.
He turns to the last page.
Tucked inside the back cover: a letter, folded small, creased as though it had been crumpled into a ball and smoothed flat again.
He unfolds it under the lamp. Cheap lined paper. Careful, laborious English handwriting.

THE LETTER

"Miss Voss. Your father did not kill himself. I can prove it. I have kept his papers for twenty years.
I am old and I am ill and I do not want to carry them any more. Please telephone." A phone number. The signature: T. SAKAI.
The envelope folded inside it is addressed to VERA VOSS.
Jack reads the letter twice. Then he looks at the name on the envelope for a long time.
The black rotary phone RINGS.
He answers. Listens.
Come back. Alone. After the last train.
The line clicks dead.

scenes.title: Montage — to the Hive, after the last train
19 — Past midnight

dialogueBeats.text: Past midnight. The shutter half down. The fluorescent tube is off; only a single bulb burns.
Kaneko lifts the curtain to the storeroom and stands aside.

scenes.title: 20 — Prove it
scenes.prose: INT. THE HIVE, NOODLE SHOP STOREROOM - CONTINUOUS

dialogueBeats.text: Flour sacks. The futon. The bare bulb.
MARA sits on the futon with her knees up and her phone to her ear, listening.
You left your umbrella. You'll get soaked.
Just call me. You don't have to say anything. Just call, so I know.
The message ends. She plays it again.
Jack is in the doorway. She scrambles back against the wall.
My name is Jack. Your sister hired me.
Prove it.

scenes.title: 20 — Prove it (cont.)

dialogueBeats.text: Jack sets her sketchbook on a flour sack between them, with the hair clip on top.
Mara stares at it.
She says it was hers. She says you stole it when you were kids and never gave it back.
Something in Mara's face gives way.
It was never hers. Dad gave it to me. She just says that.
She pulls the sketchbook into her lap.
The red bird clip lies alone on the closed cover.
She almost laughs, and then she is crying, silently, pressing the back of her wrist against her mouth.
Jack waits. He doesn't go to her. He sits down on a flour sack, slowly, making himself smaller.
Is she okay? Is she — does she know you're —
He doesn't answer. So she asks again.
Is she okay?
She's been calling you. She hasn't slept.
I know. I listen to them.
Why were you in Kanda, Mara?
She looks at him. Decides.

He wrote to Vera. Mr. Sakai. She threw it in the bin without even answering. I took it out. I called him. He said he had Dad's papers. He said to come to the bar at one o'clock. There'd be a man from a newspaper there too, so it couldn't be buried again.
I sent them both a photo so they'd know me. He wrote back one line. "You have his face."
Vera doesn't know you went.
We had a fight about it. I called her a coward. And I'm the one hiding in a storeroom. Don't tell her I'm here.
A small, bitter laugh. She hides her mouth in her sleeve.
She's your sister.

They have my purse. My passport. They know my name. They know where I live, where she lives, all of it. If she knows where I am, she'll come here. She won't be able to help it. And they'll follow her. They'll use her to get to me. And then they'll kill her too.
You don't know that.
I watched them shoot two men like they were switching off lights.

scenes.title: 20 — Prove it (cont.)

dialogueBeats.text: Silence. The bulb hums.
Promise me.
Jack looks at her for a long moment. Twenty years of silence sit behind his eyes.
I promise.

scenes.title: 21 — Footsteps on the stairs

dialogueBeats.text: Grey light. Rain on the window. Jack hasn't slept. He is in yesterday's shirt.
Footsteps on the stairs. The frosted glass. Vera's shape.
She comes in carrying two coffees in paper cups. She puts one on his desk.
You look terrible.
Thank you.
She sits. She doesn't take her coat off. She waits.
Did you find anything?
The sketchbook is on the desk between them. Jack's hand rests on its cover.
A train passes. The blinds shiver.
Not yet.
She nods. Believes him. That's the worst part.
Okay. Okay. Tomorrow, then.
She stands. At the door she hesitates, as though she wants to say something else. She doesn't. She goes.
Jack sits very still. He picks up the coffee she brought him and holds it without drinking, the way he held the can at the vending machine.

scenes.title: 22 — Somewhere like this
scenes.prose: INT. ALL-NIGHT NOODLE COUNTER, UNDER THE TRACKS - NIGHT

dialogueBeats.text: A different place: a narrow standing-and-stools counter wedged into a brick railway arch. A ticket machine by the door.
Yellowed menus on the wall. A radio behind the counter plays baseball, low.
11:40 p.m. by the clock over the door.
Vera and Jack sit side by side at the counter. Empty bowls. Two coffees in thick white cups. They have been here a long time.
Every few minutes, a train rumbles overhead, and the cups tremble in their saucers.
He used to bring us somewhere like this. Dad. After work. Mara would fall asleep on the counter and he'd carry her home.
And you?

I stayed awake. I wanted to hear everything he said to the man who made the noodles. I didn't understand any of it. I just liked that he was different here. Lighter. I think he was happy here. Before.
Jack looks down at his cup.
They said he killed himself. My mother never talked about it. Not once. We went home and it was as if Tokyo never happened.
Do you believe it?
She thinks about it for a long time.
I believe he was sad. I don't know if I believe the rest. A man wrote to me last week. He said Dad didn't do it. He said the police knew.
Jack keeps his eyes on his bowl.
What did you do?
I threw it in the bin. A stranger, after twenty years, saying he can prove it? I thought he wanted money. And if he didn't… then nobody looked. Twenty years, and nobody even looked. I couldn't.
Jack is very still. The letter is in the inside pocket of his coat. He doesn't move to touch it.
A train. The cups tremble.
You're very easy to talk to. It's annoying.
I get paid to listen.
You're not getting paid right now.
He has no answer to that.
She rests her head on her folded arms on the counter. Just for a moment. Her eyes close.
You're the first person I've trusted since she disappeared. Did you know that?
Jack looks at her. His mouth opens. The truth is right there.
Vera —
But she is asleep.
He sits and watches her breathe. A train passes. Her coffee cup, near her elbow, trembles toward the edge of the counter.
He reaches over and moves it back from the edge. Carefully. Quietly. So it won't wake her.
He doesn't wake her. He sits there until the counterman begins stacking chairs.

scenes.title: 23 — You never call
scenes.prose: EXT. YAKITORI STALL, UNDER THE TRACKS - NIGHT

dialogueBeats.text: Smoke. Red paper lanterns. Salarymen at plastic tables under a railway bridge, talking too loud.
Ishida sits alone at a corner table with a beer and a plate of skewers. Jack sits down opposite him.
You never call me unless you want something.
Sakai.
Ishida sighs. Turns a skewer over with his chopsticks.
You already know what he was. In the bubble years he cleared land. Old tenants who wouldn't sell. First he'd bring flowers. Then he'd bring men. Then something would happen. A fire, sometimes.
The Shiohama fire.

Among others. The journalist in the bar was from the Toto Shimbun. He'd been asking about the redevelopment money. Who owns what. Whose friends vote on what. The usual. Sakai called him a week ago. We think Sakai wanted to confess something before he died. He had cancer. Months left.
Confess what?
Who knows. An old man's conscience. It's very common.
Jack watches him.
Why are you telling me all this?
Ishida puts down his chopsticks.

Because you'll find out anyway. And because I would rather you heard it from me than from someone who wants to hurt you. Twenty years ago I told you to sign that report. You were young. You did what your senior told you. That was on me, not on you.
I still signed it.
And I've carried it too. Every day. Whatever Sakai hid, Jack, if you find it, bring it to me. Not to the department. To me. I'll know what to do with it this time.
Sakai had a wife.
Separated. A fishing town on the Boso coast. The police have spoken to her. She gave us nothing.
He takes a napkin, writes an address on it in careful longhand, and slides it across the table. Nothing in his face at all.
A long pause. A train roars overhead. The lanterns sway.
Jack nods slowly.
It is exactly what he needed to hear. That is what makes it dangerous.

scenes.title: 25 — The number 114
scenes.prose: INT. THE HIVE, NOODLE SHOP STOREROOM - NIGHT

dialogueBeats.text: The bulb. The flour sacks. Mara sits cross-legged on the futon. Jack sits against the opposite wall.
The curtain moves. Kaneko brings in a bowl of rice, steam rising into the bulb light.
Eat.
Thank you. Has anyone... come? Asking?
Nobody comes here who isn't lost.
She puts the bowl in Mara's hands. The curtain falls shut behind her.
The rice goes cold in Mara's lap. They talk quietly, as if the building is listening. It is.
Mr. Sakai said "twenty years." Before they shot him. Like he'd been expecting them for twenty years.
He probably had.
He knew me. He saw me in the doorway and stopped. And at the end he pressed the key into my hand. "Don't let them have it."
Jack looks down at his hands.
Beside the futon, held down by a flour scoop: a stack of loose pages covered in pencil. He turns the top one toward the bulb.
A drawing from floor level. The underside of a counter. A crate of bottles. Two pairs of shoes. A stool going over. An outflung hand.
In the corner, small: 1:07. Beside the shoes, in her careful block capitals: EXCUSE ME.
You drew this.
It's the only thing I know how to do with it. If I don't put it on paper it just keeps happening. That's what he said when he came into the bar. "Excuse me." Like a customer.
Jack sets the page down exactly where it was.
And then in the bar, the man said, "Where is he?" He was waiting for the old man. They were supposed to meet.
Sakai was bringing him something.
Mara opens her fist. The coin-locker key on its worn tag.
This.
Jack takes it. Turns it over under the bulb. The number on the worn tag, still legible: 114.
It's not a station locker. They clear those every three days.
Then what is it?
Somewhere he paid for. For a long time.
He hands it back. She looks surprised.
Keep it. Until I know what it opens. It's safer with you than with me.
Why?
Because nobody knows where you are.
Mara closes her hand around the key. She looks at him properly for the first time.
Is she eating?
What?
Vera. She forgets to eat when she's upset. She just drinks coffee. Is she eating?
Jack thinks of the counter at 11:40 p.m. The empty bowls.
Last night she had noodles.
Good. Make her eat breakfast. She never eats breakfast.

scenes.title: 25 — Breakfast
scenes.prose: INT. TINY BREAKFAST COUNTER, NEAR THE STATION - MORNING

dialogueBeats.text: A coffee counter no wider than a corridor. Six seats, a glass siphon bubbling over a flame, toast cut as thick as a paperback.
A CRT on the shelf shows a morning cooking show, sound low. The window is fogged from the inside.
Vera sits with her coat still on and her phone face up beside her, already looking at the door as though the day has started without her.
Jack sets a plate down in front of her: thick toast, a boiled egg, a small dish of pickled cabbage that nobody asked for.
Breakfast nobody asked for
What's this?
Breakfast.
I don't eat breakfast.
You drink coffee until the afternoon and then you forget to eat.
Has someone been reporting on me?
He says nothing. She looks at the plate. She looks at him. She picks up the toast, mostly to end the conversation.
You sound like my sister.
Jack's hand stops on his cup.
Vera doesn't see it. She is looking at the cooking show.
She used to stand over me with a plate. Twenty-four years old, bossing me around my own kitchen. She'd have liked you. She likes anyone who's stubborn.
She sounds like she was right.
Was. Is. I keep saying was.
Is.
She bites the toast. Chews. Her face changes, the way a person's face does when she finds out she was hungry.
She eats the egg. She eats the cabbage. On the television a chef lifts a lid and steam fills the frame.
Jack watches her eat, the way he watched her sleep.
It is the easiest hour he has spent in twenty years, and he knows exactly what it is costing.
She wipes her fingers on a paper napkin.
Thank you.
For what?
For making me.
She reaches for her purse. He is already at the till, paying. Too much. The woman behind the counter doesn't mention it.

scenes.title: 26 — The second hand

dialogueBeats.text: A green-striped commuter train circling the city. Rain on the windows. Afternoon light, grey and soft.
The carriage is half empty: schoolkids, an old man asleep, a woman with shopping.
Vera and Jack sit side by side. Nowhere to go. Just riding the loop.
Dad used to do this when he couldn't think. Ride the whole loop. An hour. He said Tokyo was a clock and the Yamanote was the second hand.
Did it help?
I don't know. He did it a lot at the end.
The train sways. Her shoulder settles against his.
She takes his hand without asking and turns it over. The old steel lighter is in his palm; he has been flicking it without knowing.
She takes it. Opens it. Closes it. Opens it.
You don't smoke.
I quit.
When?
Twenty years ago.
And you still carry the lighter.
Habit.
That's not a habit. That's a promise you don't trust yourself to keep.
He looks at her. She has no idea how true that is.
She tries to give it back. He closes her fingers around it.
Keep it.
Why?
Because I quit.
She looks at the lighter in her hand. Then she puts it in her coat pocket.
And her head comes to rest on his shoulder, as if it has always belonged there.
Out of the window, Tokyo circles past. Rooftops. Laundry. Rain.

scenes.title: 27 — The old song

dialogueBeats.text: A small intersection.
Rain.
The crossing signal turns green and the old melody begins to CHIME.
Vera and Jack cross in the rain, laughing at something, sharing his cheap plastic umbrella that's too small for two. Her shoulder gets wet.
His gets wet. Neither of them cares.
WIDE: two small figures crossing an empty road while the city's old song plays for them.

scenes.title: 27 — She was here

dialogueBeats.text: The bar in daylight again. The rubber mat is still there, still too clean. Okada is polishing a glass that is already polished.
Vera comes in without the umbrella this time. Okada sees her and doesn't say we're closed.
Mr. Okada. You said he found your daughter.
Okada goes on polishing.

She was fifteen. She went to Osaka with a boy. Everyone said she was gone. He found her in three weeks. She didn't want to come home. He telephoned me that night. Safe, he said. Tomorrow it'll be over.
Was he right?
They took her out of the river in the morning. I hated him for a year. Nobody else had even looked.
He sets the glass down.
He finds things. And then he carries them by himself. I have never seen him put anything down.
Is that a warning?
It's a description.
Vera looks along the counter, to the far end, where his eyes went the first time.
Show me where.
Okada lifts the counter flap: the gap between the crates and the ice bin.
She goes through. Crouches behind the far end, between the crates and the shelves, exactly where Mara crouched.
She sees what Mara saw: the underside of the counter, the crate of empty bottles, the place where the stool went over, the dark screen of the television on the ceiling.
She was here.
I was in the back. Moving crates. I heard all of it. I stood there with a crate in my arms and I did not move. That is why I gave you the clip. He said "excuse me" when he came in. Like a customer.
Vera stays where she is on the floor.
She would have stayed very still. She has never been still in her life.
People learn.
Vera looks up at the dead television. Somewhere in the dark glass, her own face.
For the first time she lets herself think it clearly: her sister saw two men die, and has not called.
Okada takes a card from his apron and sets it on the counter. TOTO SHIMBUN. The journalist's name in katakana: KONDO.
He left it the week before. He said he was meeting someone. He said it would be a good week. I couldn't call them. I couldn't say what I heard.
Vera takes the card.

scenes.title: 28 — The sea wall steps
scenes.prose: EXT. FISHING TOWN, BOSO COAST - DAY

dialogueBeats.text: Grey sea. Grey sky. Rain on the slipway. Boats pulled up on a concrete slipway.
A single road of low houses, their paint scoured by salt wind.
Jack's old car, parked on the sea wall. He gets out, pulls up his collar against the wind, and walks.

scenes.title: 29 — The tea she does not want to pour

dialogueBeats.text: A small room. A kotatsu table. A television with the sound off.
A Buddhist altar in the corner: a new photograph of Sakai, younger, smiling in a way that doesn't suit him.
MRS. SAKAI (70s), small and hard, pours Jack tea she doesn't want to pour.
We haven't lived together in fifteen years. The police already came.
I'm not the police.
Then what are you?
Jack thinks about it.
Someone who owes a man a debt. A long time ago. The same kind of debt your husband owed.
She studies him. Then she looks at the photograph on the altar.

He started going to temple last year. Him. Temple. He sat there for hours. I thought he'd gone soft in the head. Last month he wrote a letter. In English. Him. He made me check the spelling. To an American girl. When the doctor told him, he said he was glad. He said now he could stop being afraid of the wrong thing.
Did he ever pay rent on something? Somewhere that wasn't his home?
She looks at him sharply.
Every January. Cash, in an envelope. For years. Even after he left, the receipts kept coming here.
He left these here. Maybe on purpose.
She takes a rubber-banded bundle of receipts from the altar drawer. Carbon copies, handwritten, yellowed.
The top one: KATO RENTAL LOCKERS, UENO.
Jack unfolds it. A rubber stamp, faded. Handwritten: No. 114. Paid in full.
He looks up. She is watching him with an expression he can't read. Grief, maybe. Or relief.
Whatever it is, it was heavier than me. He carried it longer.

scenes.title: 30 — A light ahead

dialogueBeats.text: Rain. Black fields. Jack's old car, one headlight dimmer than the other, the only thing moving for miles.
Ahead, a light. A sign on a pole, half its bulbs dead: a roadside inn.

scenes.title: 31 — The only car

dialogueBeats.text: Two storeys of weathered wood and a tin roof, set back from the highway behind a gravel lot. A beer vending machine glowing by the entrance.
A faded sign. The kind of place that was modern once, in about 1975.
A pickup truck, older than the building's paint, is parked crooked behind it.
Jack pulls into the lot. The only car.

scenes.title: 32 — Just one night

dialogueBeats.text: A small, warm, faded room. A pink public payphone on the wall. A glass case of souvenir keyrings nobody has bought in decades.
A CRT television on a shelf showing a night baseball game, the crowd murmuring.
MRS. NODA (70s) comes out from the back, drying her hands. MR. NODA (70s) doesn't look away from the baseball.
Just one night?
Just one.
She hands him a heavy old key on a wooden tag.
Upstairs, at the end. The bath is shared, I'm sorry. I'll show you. The light doesn't work properly.

scenes.title: 33 — The window swollen shut
scenes.prose: INT. ROADSIDE INN, CORRIDOR AND BATH - CONTINUOUS

dialogueBeats.text: She leads him down a narrow wooden corridor. Past the kitchen: pots, a steel counter, a back door with a bolt.
Kitchen. If you want tea, just take it. The back door sticks. My husband says he'll fix it. He's said so since the Olympics.
Which Olympics?
Exactly.
She opens a door: a small tiled bathroom, a deep wooden tub, one high window over it, fogged with steam and swollen shut in its frame.
If it's too steamy, the window opens. If you hit it hard enough.
Jack notices the window. He notices everything. That is the point of the scene, and nobody in it knows it.

scenes.title: 34 — Twenty years of Januaries
scenes.prose: INT. ROADSIDE INN, JACK'S ROOM - NIGHT

dialogueBeats.text: Tatami. A low table. A thin futon already laid out. Rain loud on the tin roof.
Jack sits at the table with Sakai's receipts spread out in front of him under the lamp.
KATO RENTAL LOCKERS - UENO. No. 114. Years of Januaries.
He takes out his phone. No signal.

scenes.title: 35 — The pink payphone

dialogueBeats.text: Mr. Noda asleep in front of the baseball. Jack at the pink payphone, feeding it coins.

scenes.title: 36 — Come back safe anyway

dialogueBeats.text: Vera on the floor with her back against the bed, the apartment dark around her. Her phone rings. Unknown number. She answers fast.
Mara?
It's me.
A beat. Disappointment, then something else.
Where are you? You sound like you're calling from 1985.
The coast. An inn off the highway. The phone is pink.
She almost laughs.
Did you find anything?
Jack looks at the receipts in his hand.
Maybe. I'll know tomorrow.
Come back safe.
It's just an inn. There's an old couple and a baseball game.
Come back safe anyway.
He hears her breathing on the line. Neither of them hangs up.
The coins run out. The line goes dead.
Vera looks at the phone. Jack looks at the payphone. Both of them hold on a moment longer than they need to.

scenes.title: 37 — The keys are always in it
scenes.prose: INT. ROADSIDE INN, KITCHEN DOORWAY - NIGHT

dialogueBeats.text: Jack can't sleep. He wanders back down the corridor.
The kitchen's back door stands open to the rain. Mrs. Noda sits on the step outside under the eave, smoking.
Don't tell my husband.
I quit.
Then you'll understand why I don't want him to know.
She offers the pack anyway. He shakes his head.
He stands in the doorway and looks out: a muddy yard, a gate onto a farm track, and the old pickup parked crooked across the path.
Sorry about the truck. He parks it like he's drunk. He's never drunk. The keys are always in it. Who would steal that?
Jack looks at the truck. He says nothing.

scenes.title: 38 — Four black sedans

dialogueBeats.text: Later. 2 a.m. Rain.
The highway. Empty. Then headlights.
One car. Two. Three. Four. Black sedans, one after another, slowing, turning in, gravel crunching.

scenes.title: 50 — Hand starts to shake

dialogueBeats.text: Night. Empty highway. Rain through the shattered windscreen.
Jack drives with one hand. Blood runs from his hairline down the side of his face. His shirt is dark with it at the shoulder.
He looks in the mirror. No one.
He reaches into his jacket. The receipts are still there, soaked and creased.
He breathes. Only now does his hand start to shake.
Then the thought arrives, and his face changes.
Only two people knew where he was going tonight. He counts them silently.
Ishida. He asked Ishida for the widow's address.
And Vera. He called her from a pink payphone and told her it was just an inn.
He drives on. The wipers beat. He doesn't want to think it. He thinks it anyway.

scenes.title: 51 — The model, corrected
scenes.prose: INT. CHAIRMAN'S OFFICE, KUROSE DEVELOPMENT - DAWN

dialogueBeats.text: The fortieth floor. Glass on three sides. Tokyo spread out below in the rain like a circuit board. The glass walls grey with dawn.
Nobody in the leather chairs.
The model of the redevelopment on its long table: glass towers, sponge trees, a broad white plaza.
At the plaza's edge sits one small, dark, patched block, out of place among the towers. The Hive.
A man's hand, clean, with an expensive watch, lifts the Hive out of the model and sets it on a tray beside a cup of tea.
The plaza underneath is already finished. Tiny painted people cross it.

scenes.title: 52 — She pulls him in

dialogueBeats.text: A knock at the door. Vera opens it in a sweater, barely awake.
Jack. Soaked. Blood dried down the side of his face.
Oh my God.
She pulls him in.

scenes.title: 53 — Pink water

dialogueBeats.text: A small tiled bathroom. Jack sits on the closed toilet.
Vera kneels in front of him with a bowl of warm water and a cloth, cleaning the cut at his hairline.
He watches her face while she works. Very closely. As though he is trying to read something written there.
Who did this?
I don't know.
You don't know?
Two that I saw. Masks. They didn't introduce themselves.
She wrings out the cloth.
Pink water.
You told me it was just an inn.
It was just an inn.
Jack's eyes go to Vera's phone on the edge of the bath,
where it has sat all night in case Mara calls. He stops.
She looks up and catches him watching her.
What is it?
He doesn't answer. He's still watching. Measuring.
She sees something in his look that she doesn't understand, and it frightens her more than the blood.
Jack. What!
He looks at her hands: careful, steady, stained pink. At her face: exhausted, afraid for him.
Whatever he was looking for, it isn't there. It was never there.
Nothing. I'm sorry. Nothing.
She puts a plaster on the cut, very gently. Her hand stays on his face a moment after.
He covers her hand with his.
And then, without either of them deciding, she kisses him. Or he kisses her. It doesn't matter which.
It is quiet, and brief, and it changes everything.
When it ends, she rests her forehead against his.
Don't go anywhere else without telling me.
I won't.
When she turns to wring out the cloth, he reaches over and turns her phone face-down.
It is another promise. He is collecting them.

scenes.title: Montage — the night after Pink water
53 — There was no car

dialogueBeats.text: An old newspaper office. Stacks of paper. Desks jammed together. Televisions on the walls showing three different channels.
Nobody under fifty looks up from a screen.
Vera stands at the door of a glass-walled office at the back, KONDO's card in her hand.
HARADA (50s), the editor, grey-haired, sleeves rolled, is finishing a call. She sees the card and ends it without hurry.
On her desk, a framed photograph of the journalist from the bar, laughing at an office party.
You're not a reporter.
My sister was in that bar.
Harada looks at her for a long time. Then at the photograph. She points at the chair.
We have had a letter from lawyers already. Kondo was six months on the redevelopment money. Who owns what. Whose friends sit on which committee. He never touched a gang in his life.
The police say it's a gang matter.
The police say what they are told.
Did he say who he was meeting?
One o'clock, Kanda, an old man who wanted to talk. He told two people. Me. And a detective.
Which detective?
He didn't say. He said the detective had promised to keep a car nearby. There was no car.
Vera sits very still.
Will you print it?
Print what? A dead man's diary? Bring me something with a name on it.
Vera writes her number on the back of Kondo's card and leaves it on the desk, beside the photograph.

scenes.title: 54 — Everything is still there

dialogueBeats.text: A tiny kiosk wedged into the corner of a shopping arcade.
An OLD TOBACCONIST (80s) behind a window full of cigarette cartons and lottery tickets.
Vera holds up the old photograph. The American man, two small girls, the noodle shop sign.
My father worked near here, a long time ago. Do you know this place?
The tobacconist puts on his glasses. Looks. Smiles with all his remaining teeth.
Kaneko's. Of course. In the Hive. Not for long, though. They're knocking it all down.
Vera stares at him.
It's still there?
Everything is still there. Until it isn't.

scenes.title: 55 — They match

dialogueBeats.text: Vera walks through the narrow corridors with the photograph in her hand, looking at everything as though she's trying to remember it.
Bare bulbs. Dripping water. The radio repairman's dozen murmuring stations. Daylight falls in thin cold shafts through the steam.
At a turning she stops, then takes the left without looking, the way you take a stair you've climbed a thousand times.
A hand-painted sign for a DENTIST, one flight up. A RADIO REPAIRMAN at his bench under a bare bulb glances up at her and back down.
Through a half-open door, an OLD WOMAN watches sumo on a television the size of a bread box.
Vera puts her hand flat on the wall, low, where a child's hand would reach.
A train passes overhead. The building trembles.
She stops. Turns a corner.
The noodle counter. The sign.
She stands there for a long moment, holding the photograph up beside the real thing. They match.

scenes.title: 56 — The third stool

dialogueBeats.text: Lunchtime. Steam. Three customers.
Vera sits at the counter.
Kaneko turns from the pot, glances at her, and goes on working.
I'm sorry, I don't know what to order. I was here when I was a child. With my father. He always sat here.
She takes the old photograph from her bag and sets it on the counter: the American man, two small girls, the noodle shop sign.
Kaneko looks at the photograph for a long moment. Then at Vera. She freezes, just for a second.
He always paid too much.
Vera's breath catches.
You remember him?
And you. You ate everything on his plate.
She sets a bowl of noodles in front of Vera. Vera looks at it. Her eyes fill.

scenes.title: 57 — Three feet away
scenes.prose: INT. THE HIVE, NOODLE SHOP STOREROOM - CONTINUOUS

dialogueBeats.text: On the other side of the curtain, three feet away.
Mara stands pressed against the wall with both hands over her mouth. She has heard her sister's voice. She is shaking.
Through the thin gap at the edge of the curtain she can see the back of Vera's head.
Mara takes one step toward the curtain. Her hand lifts to it.
She stops.
She thinks of the purse in the rain. Of the two men falling. Of her sister being followed through these corridors.
Her hand drops.

scenes.title: 58 — Bring her

dialogueBeats.text: Vera eats. All of it. She laughs once, at nothing, wiping her eyes.
My sister would love this place. She's never seen it. She only knows it from my stories. When I find her, I'll bring her here.
Kaneko's chopsticks stop moving in the pot. She doesn't look up.
Yes. Bring her.
Vera puts money on the counter. Too much. Kaneko notices and says nothing.
Vera goes, lighter than she has been for the whole film.
Behind the curtain, Mara slides down the wall to the floor.

scenes.title: 59 — It rings. Nobody answers.

dialogueBeats.text: Rain. By the Hive's narrow entrance, under a tin awning, a green public payphone. JACK stands at it with the receiver to his ear.
It's ringing.

MRS. SAKAI'S HOUSE

The kotatsu.
The altar. The television on with the sound off.
A teacup on its side on the tatami.
The phone rings in the empty room.

THE HIVE

It rings. Nobody answers. He hangs up. He walks a few steps down the street in the rain, then turns back.
Vera comes out of the Hive's narrow entrance, glowing. She sees him walking back to her.
Jack! It's still here. The noodle shop from the photo. It's real. The same woman — she remembered Dad. She remembered me.
Jack hardly hears her. He looks back at the payphone.
And I went to the newspaper. Harada, the editor. She says Kondo told two people about the one o'clock. Her. And a detective, who promised to keep a car nearby.
Later.
Jack. A detective.
Later. Please.
When we find Mara, I'm bringing her here. She'll finally see it.
Yes.

scenes.title: 60 — I want my sister
scenes.prose: INT. THE HIVE, NOODLE SHOP STOREROOM - NIGHT

dialogueBeats.text: The bulb. Mara sits on the futon with her knees pulled up. Her face is swollen from crying.
On the wall beside her, taped up with rice-paper tape: a new drawing, still smudged. The noodle counter from behind the curtain.
The back of a head.
Jack crouches in front of her.
She was right there. She was right there and I —
You did the right thing.
Did I? She said she'd bring me here. When she finds me. She was so happy.
She wipes her face with the heel of her hand.
If she found this place, other people can.
I know.
Find what it opens. And then this ends. I don't want to hide any more. I want my sister.
She takes the key from around her neck, on a shoelace, and puts it in his hand. Its worn tag reads 114.
Tomorrow night I'm moving you out of here. Somewhere safe, outside Tokyo. A police car and a house. Someone I trust.
And then?
And then I tell her everything.
Mara looks at him. She believes him.

scenes.title: 61 — Nine o'clock

dialogueBeats.text: Parked under an elevated expressway. Rain drumming on the roof. The dashboard glow.
Ishida behind the wheel. Jack in the passenger seat. Neither looks at the other.
The inn. I heard this morning. Thank God. The widow's file went through the department the day I pulled it. Someone read it. I am looking for him.
Jack studies the side of his face. It is the answer he needs.
I have a witness. From the bar.
A pause. Ishida's expression doesn't change at all. That is the tell, and only we know it.
The sister.
I need a safe car. A safe house outside the city. No paperwork. No department. Just you.
When?
Tomorrow night.
Ishida nods slowly, as if thinking it through. As if it costs him something.
Nine o'clock. The service road behind the Hive, by the railway pillars. A grey car. My driver. I'll arrange the house myself. And Sakai's thing?
Jack turns and looks at him. Ishida keeps his eyes on the rain on the windscreen.
Where else would the Voss girl go? You took me there yourself. Twenty years ago.
Jack looks at Ishida's hands on the wheel. He doesn't ask.
I'll bring it to you. When she's safe.
Good. You've done well, Jack. This time you've done well.
Jack looks out at the rain. For the first time in twenty years, he lets himself believe it.

scenes.title: 62 — Like a date

dialogueBeats.text: The same small intersection as before. The signal is red. Vera and Jack stand at the kerb under his cheap plastic umbrella.
Tomorrow night. Will you have dinner with me?
She looks at him, surprised.
Like a date?
Like a date.
Jack, my sister —
I know.
There's something I need to tell you. I want to tell you properly. Not in an office. Not on a train.
She searches his face. Whatever she finds there makes her smile. Properly. For the first time in the film.
Okay.
The old hotel by the station. The lounge. Ten o'clock.
Ten o'clock.
The signal turns green. The old melody begins to CHIME.
They cross. She takes his arm.

scenes.title: 63 — No questions
scenes.prose: INT. KATO RENTAL LOCKERS, UENO - NIGHT

dialogueBeats.text: A narrow room under a railway arch, lined floor to ceiling with battered grey steel lockers, each one numbered in fading paint.
A single fluorescent tube. A sign in faded letters: MONTHLY. YEARLY. NO QUESTIONS.
At a desk by the door, a CARETAKER (80s) sleeps with his head on a ledger.
Jack opens a locker with Mara's key. Inside: a padded envelope, taped shut.
Under it, a small black notebook, water-stained, its cover gone soft with age.
In the envelope, a single cassette tape in a cracked plastic case, labelled in a shaking hand: SHIOHAMA.
He opens the notebook. English handwriting. On the flyleaf: DANIEL VOSS.
Jack stands very still.
He turns pages. The handwriting grows faster, more anxious. And then a page near the end, and a line underlined twice.
He reads it. We don't see what it says. We see his face.
He closes it. The notebook goes inside his coat. The envelope he carries in his hand.
A train passes overhead. The lockers rattle in their rows, all of them at once, like a room full of doors being tried.

scenes.title: 63 — Not another day
scenes.prose: EXT. UENO, UNDER THE RAILWAY ARCHES - NIGHT

dialogueBeats.text: A row of brick arches with shops in them: shuttered, lit, shuttered. Rain running down the ironwork.
Jack comes out of the locker room with his coat buttoned over the notebook and something flat inside it.
At the far end of the arch, a black sedan sits with its lights off and its engine running.
Jack doesn't look at it. He walks.
Behind him, the sedan's lights come on. It follows at walking pace.
He turns into a doorway of noise: a PACHINKO PARLOUR, a wall of steel balls and light and a hundred people staring at their machines.
He walks straight through, between the rows, out through the fire door at the back and into an alley of dripping air conditioners.
He waits. Watches the far end of the alley.
Two men in dark coats run past the mouth of it, scanning, and are gone.
Behind them, in the street, the sedan crawls along the kerb and stops. Someone inside is speaking into a sleeve. We can't hear it.
We can see him give up.
A last train pulls out overhead. The arches shake.
Jack takes the cassette from inside his coat and looks at it, in the light of a vending machine.
He can't carry it any more. Not another day.

scenes.title: 64 — Behind the counter

dialogueBeats.text: Okada's bar. Late. No customers. The CRT television is off.
Jack slides the cassette case across the counter.
Keep this for me. Don't tell anyone. Not the police. Not me, if I ask you with someone standing behind me.
Okada looks at the tape. Then he takes it, lifts the lid of the old cash drawer, removes the tray, and puts the tape underneath.
Behind the counter. Like the girl's clip.
The girl?
He pours Jack a drink. Jack doesn't drink it.
Safe. Tomorrow it'll be over.
You said that about my daughter.

scenes.title: 65 — The wine-red dress

dialogueBeats.text: Rain on the window. The last grey light.
Vera stands on a chair and lifts down a flat cardboard box from the top of the wardrobe. Dust on the lid.
Her mother's handwriting on the side, in marker: TOKYO.
She opens it on the bed.
Inside, folded in tissue paper that has gone yellow: a dress. Wine red. Silk.
The kind of dress a young woman wore to an expensive restaurant in 1990 and never wore again.
Vera holds it up against herself in the mirror. For a moment she is someone else. Her mother, maybe.

scenes.title: 65 — The wine-red dress (cont.)

dialogueBeats.text: Through the thin wall, the neighbour's radio begins to play the same old ballad from before: the woman's voice.
LATER:
Vera at the small mirror by the window, in the red dress, doing her makeup. She is out of practice.
She wipes off the lipstick and does it again. Her hands aren't quite steady.
She looks at herself for a long time. She almost looks happy. She doesn't quite trust it.
She picks up her bag. Puts in her phone. Then, after a moment, the old steel lighter.
At the door she stops by the umbrella stand. The pale blue umbrella.
She takes it.
Borrowing it. You'll get it back.
She goes. Through the wall, the song plays on.

scenes.title: 66 — Waiting for someone

dialogueBeats.text: An old hotel built in the Showa years for a future that never quite came. Amber light. Brass rails. Deep leather chairs.
Bottles glowing behind the bar like a shrine.
In the corner, a PIANIST (60s) in a white jacket plays standards, softly, to almost no one.
A clock above the bar: 9:58.
Vera comes in, shaking the rain from the blue umbrella. People turn to look at her, briefly.
She is beautiful and doesn't know where to put her hands.
She sits at the bar. Leans the blue umbrella against the next stool.
For you?
I'm waiting for someone. A gin and tonic. Please.
She looks at the door.
The clock: 10:00.

scenes.title: 67 — A different clock
scenes.prose: EXT. SERVICE ROAD BEHIND THE HIVE - NIGHT

dialogueBeats.text: Earlier. The clock is a different clock here: 8:52 on a lit sign above a closed garage.
A narrow road running under the elevated railway. A row of massive concrete pillars. Puddles. One sodium lamp.
A grey sedan waits beside the pillars, engine running, wipers slow.

scenes.title: 68 — Rice balls for the car
scenes.prose: INT. THE HIVE, NOODLE SHOP STOREROOM - CONTINUOUS

dialogueBeats.text: Mara puts on a borrowed coat.
She has a small cloth bag: a toothbrush, the cardigan, the sketchbook pages she tore from the wall, all but the drawings from behind the curtain, which she leaves taped where they are.
The loose pages of the bar, drawn from the floor, she folds in four and puts in the bag with the rest.
Kaneko stands in the curtain. She hands Mara a small parcel wrapped in newspaper.
Rice balls. For the car.
Mara takes them. She doesn't know what to say.
Thank you. For —
Come back with your sister. Sit on the stools. Both of you. Eat everything.
Mara bows, too deep, clumsy. Kaneko, unexpectedly, puts a hand on her head. Just for a second. Like a grandmother.
It's time.

scenes.title: 69 — Vera would love this

dialogueBeats.text: Jack leads Mara through the narrow corridors. Bare bulbs. Dripping pipes.
The radio repairman looks up from his bench as they pass, and nods.
Doors open onto other lives. A family watching television. A man asleep. A girl practising the violin, badly.
Mara looks at all of it as if memorising it.
Vera would love this.
You can bring her.
When it's over, you'll tell her? Everything?
Tonight. I'm meeting her at ten.
She stops walking. Looks at him.
Meeting her?
For dinner.
Mara studies him. And then, for the first time, she smiles. A real one. Her sister's smile.
Oh. Oh, I see.
It's not —
It is. It's fine. It's good. She deserves someone who looks for things.
A train passes overhead. The building trembles. They walk on.

scenes.title: 70 — Position
scenes.prose: EXT. SERVICE ROAD BEHIND THE HIVE - CONTINUOUS

dialogueBeats.text: Jack and Mara come out of a narrow back door of the Hive into the rain.
The grey sedan waits beside the pillars, twenty metres away. A DRIVER in a dark coat gets out and opens the rear door for them. Polite.
Professional. He bows slightly as they come.
Jack walks Mara toward it. Halfway there.
Shitsurei shimasu. (Excuse me.)
He says it the way you would to a passenger.
Mara stops dead.
She has heard those words before. From the floor of a bar, before two shots.
That's them.
What?
That's what he said. Before he shot him. "Excuse me."
The driver lifts his wrist to his mouth and murmurs into his sleeve, very quietly:
Position.
Jack looks at the driver. The driver looks at Jack. And in that look, both men understand.
Jack shoves Mara back toward the Hive door.
Run!
From the dark between the pillars: muzzle flashes. Suppressed shots, flat and ordinary.
Jack draws Mara down behind a dumpster. Rounds clang off the steel. The driver pulls a weapon from his coat.
Mara breaks for the Hive door. Five metres. Three.
A shot.
She stumbles. Keeps going. Falls through the doorway.
Jack goes after her, low, as bullets chew the doorframe above his head.

scenes.title: 71 — Everyone's awake

dialogueBeats.text: Jack drags the door shut behind him and throws the bolt. Pounding on the door. Shots through it, splintering the wood.
Mara is on the floor of the narrow passage, her back against the wall. She is holding her side. Her hand is dark and wet.
Jack kneels, presses his hands over hers.
Stay with me. Mara. Stay with me.
Above them, a window opens. Then another.
Lights snap on, one after another, up through the whole building: the thousand windows of the Hive waking.
Outside, a car door slams. An engine revs. Tyres on wet asphalt. Going.
And far away, finally, sirens.
Mara looks up at all the light.
Everyone's awake.
Yes. Everyone's awake. Help's coming.
Mara's hand finds his wrist. Her grip is weak.
Jack.
I'm here.
Tell her I'm sorry.
You'll tell her. Tonight. I'll bring her here, you can —
Tell her.
Doors open along the passage.
Faces in the bulb light: the RADIO REPAIRMAN in his vest, the OLD WOMAN from the sumo room, KANEKO running, still in her apron.
Mara's cloth bag has split open on the floor. Rice balls. A toothbrush. The cardigan.
Pages of drawings, soaking in the thin shining stream that runs along the floor.
While Jack holds Mara, Kaneko kneels and begins, very carefully, to pick up the pages. The old woman kneels beside her and helps.
Her eyes stay on the lights above. Then they stop moving.
Jack doesn't let go of her hand.
Kaneko sinks down beside them in the narrow passage. She doesn't cry.
She takes off her apron and folds it and places it gently under Mara's head, as though that still matters.
A train passes overhead. The bulbs swing. The whole building trembles, the way it always does.

scenes.title: 72 — The call

dialogueBeats.text: The clock above the bar: 11:52.
Vera's gin and tonic sits untouched. The ice has melted. The lime has sunk.
The pianist plays something slow. The same old ballad from the neighbour's radio, only now on a piano, stripped of its words.
Vera looks at the door. At her phone. No messages.
She takes out the lighter and turns it over in her fingers. Open. Shut.
Another?
No. Thank you.
She almost laughs at herself. She looks down at the red dress. She feels foolish, and then hurt, and then angry.
Her phone RINGS.
She grabs it. The screen: ISHIDA.
Her face changes. She answers.
Hello?
Miss Voss. I'm so sorry to call so late.
She knows. From his voice, she already knows. She stands up.
Your sister was found tonight. I'm very sorry. She died a short time ago.
