scenes.title: 77 — The envelope (after the song)

dialogueBeats.text: He opens the drawer. Takes out a clean envelope.
Takes Sakai's letter from his coat, smooths it once more along its crease, and folds it inside the notebook's cover.
Puts the notebook in the envelope.
He picks up a pen to write something on the envelope. He holds it over the paper for a long time.
He writes nothing.

scenes.title: 77 — The black glass

dialogueBeats.text: Before dawn. A wide avenue of shuttered banks and dark office lobbies. White streetlights in a long straight row, each one the same.
Rain on the asphalt. Nobody.
Jack walks with the envelope flat inside his jacket. He still hasn't washed his hands.
Headlights behind him. A long black sedan comes up slowly and keeps his pace. He doesn't look at it.
The rear window comes down. The back seat is dark. A man's hand rests on the sill: clean, with the watch from the model.
His face stays in the dark.
Detective.
Not any more.
No. I was sorry to hear about the girl.
Jack keeps walking. Inside his jacket, his hand closes on the envelope.
You were a sensible policeman, I'm told. You always knew when to stop.
Maybe that was a mistake.
Everyone is allowed one.
The window rises. In the black glass, Jack sees only his own face.
The sedan pulls ahead without hurry and turns off into the dark.
Jack stands in the rain a moment. Then he walks on, the way he was going.

scenes.title: 78 — No name
scenes.prose: EXT. VERA'S APARTMENT BUILDING, CORRIDOR - DAWN

dialogueBeats.text: Grey light. An open-air walkway along the third floor. Rain dripping from the railing.
Jack at Vera's door. He knocks once.
He sets the envelope on the mat, squares it to the door, and walks away.
Vera opens her door. She is still in the dress. She hasn't slept.
On the doormat: a plain envelope. No name.
She picks it up. Opens it. The cloth-covered notebook. And tucked inside its cover, a folded sheet of lined paper.
She sees the name inside the cover, and her whole body goes still.
DANIEL VOSS.

scenes.title: 79 — Her father's handwriting

dialogueBeats.text: Vera sits at the low table in the dawn light. Beside her, the two cups from the beginning of the film, both empty now.
She unfolds the lined paper first.
Careful, laborious English handwriting. "Miss Voss. Your father did not kill himself. I can prove it."
It is the letter she threw away. Smoothed flat by someone else's hands.
She understands, all at once, why her sister was in a Kanda backstreet at one in the morning.
Mara went to find the truth Vera refused to look at.
She sets the letter down very carefully, beside the empty cups. Then she opens the notebook and turns the pages.
Her father's handwriting. Neat, slanted, careful.
Shiohama. Third visit. The residents say men came in the spring with flowers, and then in the summer with iron bars. The fire began in two places at once. Fires don't do that.
She turns pages. The handwriting grows faster.
The claim will be paid. Everyone wants it paid. The company, the police, the man who owns the land now. Kurose. Always Kurose.
Pages.
The police have given me a young detective who speaks English. They call him Jack. He's bright. He believes me. We ate noodles at Kaneko's and I told him everything and he wrote it all down.
Vera stops. Reads that line again.
Her hand goes to her mouth.
She turns the page. The line we didn't see Jack read, underlined twice.
Today Jack signed the report. Accidental fire. I don't blame him. He is twenty-eight years old and they own his whole life. But I thought, of all of them, he would stand with me.
Vera stares at the page.
I'll go on alone. I've done it before.
The last pages. The handwriting is almost unrecognisable now.
They followed me home again tonight. The girls were asleep. I stood at the door a long time. If something happens to me, it will not be what they say.
Vera closes the notebook.
For twenty years she believed her father chose to leave her.
She sits in the grey light, holding the notebook against her chest, the way she held the lighter.
She has been given back her father and taken Jack away in the same hour. She doesn't know which to feel first.

scenes.title: 80 — Where to find them
scenes.prose: INT. POLICE STATION, DETECTIVES' ROOM - DAY

dialogueBeats.text: Rows of cluttered desks, most of them empty: the shift change.
Two young detectives at the far end, heads down over paperwork, too far away to hear. On the wall, the clock that runs a minute fast.
Ishida sits at his desk writing a report in careful longhand.
Jack walks the length of the room. The young detectives glance up and then look away. He hasn't shaved.
There is still dried blood in the creases of his knuckles.
He stops at Ishida's desk. Ishida doesn't look up.
Nine o'clock. A grey car. Your driver.
Ishida finishes his sentence. Puts down the pen.
Only you knew.
A long pause.
You told me yourself, Jack. You always tell the wrong person.
Jack's hands close at his sides. The far end of the room has gone quiet.
Twenty years ago. Daniel. Was that you?
I have never killed anyone in my life. I only ever told people where to find them.
Jack looks at him for a long time. Ishida almost seems to want him to.
He does.
Jack hits him. Ishida doesn't lift his hands. Jack hits him again, and again. The chair goes over. Papers slide off the desk.
At the far end of the room, the two young detectives are on their feet.
From the floor, Ishida lifts one hand. Not to Jack. To them. They stay where they are.
Jack stands over him, breathing hard. His knuckles are bleeding again.
Ishida wipes his mouth with the back of his hand. Looks at the blood on it. Then up at Jack.
Where is it? Sakai's thing.
Jack turns and walks away down the long room, past the desks, past the clock.
Ishida watches him go. For the first time, he looks afraid.

scenes.title: 81 — Without a toast

dialogueBeats.text: The bar in daylight. Chairs on the tables. Okada behind the counter.
He sees Jack's face and his hands, and he doesn't ask. He opens the cash drawer, lifts out the tray, and hands Jack the cassette.
Jack holds it.
The girl?
Jack can't answer.
Okada closes his eyes. Then he pours two small glasses and puts one in front of Jack. They drink together, without a toast.

scenes.title: 82 — Start with my part

dialogueBeats.text: An old newspaper office. Stacks of paper. Desks jammed together. Televisions on the walls showing three different channels.
Nobody under fifty looks up from a screen.
In a glass-walled office at the back: HARADA (50s), the editor, grey-haired, sleeves rolled.
On her desk, a framed photo of the JOURNALIST from the bar, laughing at some office party.
Jack walks in through the glass doors, determined. He doesn't stop.
He comes down the aisle between the desks, eyes on the glass office at the back.
Nobody stops him.
He reaches the glass office without slowing.
On the desk between them: an old cassette player, borrowed from somewhere, and the tape.
Harada presses PLAY.
Hiss. Then two men's voices, twenty years younger. Sakai's rough. The other one smooth, patient, faintly bored.
There are still people in the building. Old people. They won't sign.
The building must be empty by the end of the month.
And if it isn't?
Then it will be empty in a different way. Don't make me say it more clearly, Sakai. I don't like to repeat myself.
Harada stops the tape. The newsroom noise outside the glass seems very far away.
That's Kurose.
That's Kurose.
A voice on a twenty-year-old tape. His lawyers will say it's a fake. They'll say Sakai was a gangster with a grudge.
Then you'll need a witness.
She looks at him.

Twenty years ago I was a police detective. An American insurance investigator named Daniel Voss proved the Shiohama fire was arson. I believed him. I was ordered to close the case, and I signed a report saying the fire was an accident. Weeks later he was found dead. I didn't ask any questions.
You understand what you're saying. You'll be named. Your part too.
Start with my part.
Harada looks at him for a long moment. Then she looks at the photograph of her dead reporter on the desk.
She takes a notebook from her drawer and opens it to a clean page.
From the beginning.
Jack begins to talk. We don't hear it.
We watch him through the glass wall of her office, among the busy desks and flickering televisions: a man, for the first time in twenty years, not silent.

scenes.title: 82 — The notebook photocopied
scenes.prose: INT. TOTO SHIMBUN NEWSROOM, CORRIDOR - LATER

dialogueBeats.text: Vera stands at the edge of the newsroom with a plain folder under her arm and her father's notebook in both hands.
Through the glass wall of the office at the back, Jack, talking. She can't hear him. She has never seen him say anything true in that voice.
She doesn't go in.
A YOUNG COPY CLERK at a photocopier lays the notebook open under the lid and presses the button.
A bar of light passes under the page: her father's handwriting, flashing white. Turn. Press. Turn. Press.
Harada comes out of the office and pulls the door closed behind her.
Two hours. He hasn't stopped.
I know. I can see.
Harada watches the pages come out of the machine.
Every page. Then the original goes in the safe downstairs, and nobody touches it. Including you.
It's all I have of him.

Then I will take care of it. Kondo's files were in his desk. Six months of redevelopment money, and Kurose's name in most of it. And the grey car that left the Hive last night was found burnt out in Adachi at dawn. Registered to a security company. The company belongs to Kurose Development. Tomorrow we put it to them for comment. They will refuse to see a reporter.
I'll go.
That is not your job.
It isn't yours either. He'll see me. He'll want to look at me.
Harada studies her. Then hands her the folder: a stack of photocopies, warm from the machine.
The copies. Not the original.

scenes.title: 83 — It's just a face
scenes.prose: INT. CHAIRMAN'S OFFICE, KUROSE DEVELOPMENT - DAY

dialogueBeats.text: The fortieth floor. Rain on the glass. Tokyo grey and endless below.
Vera sits in a leather chair in front of Kurose's desk. She wears a plain dark coat.
A plain folder is on her lap, her hands flat on its cover: photocopies of every page of her father's notebook.
Across from her sits THE CHAIRMAN, KUROSE (70s). Silver hair. A beautiful suit. The stillness of a man who has never had to hurry.
Courteous. Curious. He pours her tea himself.
When my secretary said the daughter of Daniel Voss wanted to see me, I didn't believe her.
His English is perfect. Old-fashioned.
He sat where you're sitting. He looked at me the way you are. As if I'd done something.
Did you?
To him? I don't remember. Your father was a good man, Miss Voss. I mean that sincerely. There are not many. Good men are very expensive.
Vera doesn't touch the tea.
What is it you want?
He takes a plain envelope, thick with cash, from a drawer and lays it on the glass between them. She doesn't look at it.
The Toto Shimbun will print tomorrow. They asked me to bring you the chance to reply.
And they sent you.
I said I'd come.
Why?
I wanted to see your face.
And?
It's just a face.
For the first time, something flickers in him. Not fear. Irritation, perhaps, at being looked at like that.
Vera stands. She holds up a page of the photocopy. Not threatening. Just showing it to him.
My father kept notes. He wrote your name on every page. And now I know.
She walks to the door. On her way out, she stops at the model. Where the Hive stood, there's only the white plaza.
Tiny painted people cross it.
It's very clean.
She goes.
Kurose sits still for a moment. Then he presses a button on his desk phone.
Follow her.

scenes.title: 84 — Three feet away
scenes.prose: INT. THE HIVE, NOODLE SHOP STOREROOM - NIGHT

dialogueBeats.text: The bulb. The flour sacks. The futon, folded now. On it, a neat stack of drawings, dried flat, their edges rippled from the wet floor.
Jack sits on the floor against the wall. He has been hiding here since the newspaper; he can't go home. His face is grey with exhaustion.
The curtain opens. Kaneko.
Someone for you.
She stands aside.
Vera.
Jack gets to his feet. Neither of them moves toward the other.
She asked me to come. Kaneko. She said I should see where Mara was.
In her hands, a small cloth bag with one strap frayed. Kaneko put it there at the door.
She looks around the tiny room. The bare bulb. The flour sacks.
And on the wall, taped up with rice-paper tape, pages from Mara's sketchbook: drawings of the noodle counter, but from the inside now.
From behind the curtain. The back of a head.
Vera walks to the wall. Looks at the drawing for a long time.
That's me.
She drew it after you left.
She was here. The day I came.
Right behind the curtain.
Vera touches the paper with one finger.
And you told her not to come out.
She told herself. She was protecting you. So was I.
Ishida called me before it was on any news. He knew exactly where she was.
I told him. Where she'd be, and when. He arranged the car. It was his driver. That's mine.
I trusted him. I'm so sorry.
I told you about the detective. The one who promised a car. You never asked who.
No.
Vera says nothing for a while. She does not say it's all right.
I'm not going to tell you it wasn't yours.
Don't.
She opens the bag. Folded pages, soft with handling. She smooths one flat on the flour sack: a counter seen from the floor.
Two pairs of shoes. A stool going over. A hand. Beside the shoes, in block capitals: EXCUSE ME.
She drew what she saw. All of it.
She never told me she'd kept them.
I'm taking these to Harada. Somebody has to look at them. I read his notebook.
I know.
He didn't blame you.
I know.
I don't know if I'm as good as he was.
No one's asking you to be.
Silence. A train passes overhead. The bulb swings.
And under the train, so quietly it's almost part of it: in the passage outside, a man's voice, murmuring into his sleeve.
Position.
Jack's head snaps round. Vera sees his face and understands.
The bulb goes on swinging.

scenes.title: 98 — The rain has stopped
scenes.prose: EXT. ROOFTOP OF JACK'S BUILDING - DAY

dialogueBeats.text: FIVE DAYS LATER
The rain has stopped. The sky is pale and washed and enormous.
A small flat roof: laundry poles, a water tank, a single potted plant someone has kept alive.
Below, the elevated railway, and the trains going past at eye level.
Jack stands at the railing. He hears the door behind him.
Vera. In a plain coat. Her hair dry.
She comes to stand beside him at the railing. Not close. Not far.
Mom flies home tonight. She's taking Mara with her.
Jack doesn't answer for a while.
I told her you were with her at the end.
I was.
And you?
I give my statement to the prosecutors on Monday. They suspended my licence yesterday. It should have gone twenty years ago.
Ishida left a note. In his car. It says he acted alone.
Is that what it says?
That's what the police say it says.
A train passes below. They watch it.
Jack takes something from his pocket. Holds it out on his open palm.
The red bird clip.
This is yours.
Vera looks at it. She takes it.
She told me your dad gave it to her. That you only say it was yours.
Vera laughs. It comes out broken.
Liar. It was mine.
She closes her hand around it.
Jack looks at the trains. It is the hardest thing he will ever say, and he says it simply.
I promised her I'd tell you everything when it was over. This is the last of it. At the end, she said, "Tell her I'm sorry."
Vera goes very still.
And then she understands. Not the words. What they mean. The fight. The word coward. The flight home.
Everything Vera has carried since the first scene, Mara was carrying too. They were both sorry, and neither of them said it.
Vera turns away to the railing. Her shoulders shake. Jack doesn't touch her.
He stands beside her while she cries, the way he knelt beside her in the rain. Close enough. Not closer.
When she can speak:
I'm not flying home with Mom tonight.
Jack looks at her.
Somebody from Mara's family should walk in with you on Monday.
You don't have to.
I know.
A train. They watch it pass.
I don't know what we are.
Neither do I.
I still have your lighter.
I know.
She takes it from her coat pocket. Looks at it. Opens it. Closes it.
She doesn't give it back. She puts it away again.
Kaneko's opening a new place. Near the station, under the arches. She's taking the sign.
She walks to the rooftop door. Stops. Doesn't look back.
She says she opens at six.
She goes.
Jack stands alone at the railing. A train passes, its windows full of people.
For a moment, in one of the windows, the reflection of his own face.

scenes.title: 99 — The Hive coming down, then the plaza
scenes.prose: EXT. THE HIVE / THE PLAZA, WHERE THE HIVE WAS - DAY

dialogueBeats.text: Weeks later.
The Hive is coming down.
Excavators bite into the walls with long steel jaws. Concrete falls in slow grey curtains. Dust hangs in the air.
The building has been cut open like the illustrated cross-sections in an old book.
Rooms stand exposed to the sky, stacked one above another: a wall of flowered wallpaper, a calendar still pinned beside a window, a mirror, a child's height marks pencilled on a doorframe.
The camera tracks slowly sideways along the ruined face of the building, as it tracked along the lit windows of the living one.
Empty room after empty room. We remember who lived in each.
At ground level, Kaneko's counter is still standing. Its six old stools in a row.
At the barrier on the street, a small crowd watches. The radio repairman. The family. The girl with the violin case.
Kaneko stands among them, holding the old noodle-shop sign against her chest, wrapped in a blanket.
Months later. Winter light, thin and clear. No rain.
The white plaza from the model, built.
Real people cross it now, exactly like the painted ones. A strip of new grass. A bench nobody sits on.
Nothing marks where anything was.

scenes.title: 100 — The city goes on

dialogueBeats.text: A tiny place in a brick railway arch near the station. Steam. One warm bulb.
Above the counter, the old hand-painted sign. Faded. Unmistakable.
A train goes over. The bottles tick against each other and settle.
On a shelf above the door, a small old television with the sound down: the evening news.
KUROSE walking into a building between lawyers, cameras flashing, his face composed. A photograph of ISHIDA in uniform. Then the weather.
Nobody looks up.
Kaneko ladles. JACK sits at the counter, a bowl in front of him, a space beside him.
The curtain in the doorway moves. VERA. The red bird clip in her hair.
She stands a moment. Then she sits down beside him.
Kaneko sets a bowl in front of her. Vera eats. All of it.
She puts money on the counter. Too much. Kaneko looks at it, then at her, and leaves it where it is.
Past the curtain: a lit window, a radio through a wall, the city going on.
The three of them in the steam.
